quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 operating earnings of $1.64 per share, or $891 million, versus $1.54 per share in Q1 2025; full-year 2026 operating earnings guidance of $6.15-$6.45 per share reaffirmed, along with the 7%-9% operating earnings growth rate for 2026 through 2030. CFO Trevor Mihalik: regulated earned ROE for the quarter increased to 9.3% and is expected to reach approximately 9.5% by 2030; VIU and T&D segments strong on rate case outcomes, partly offset by prior-year favorable weather; Transmission Holdco hit by storm restoration and higher property taxes but expected to be favorable year over year by end of 2026.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 2026 operating EPS $1.64 ($891 million) vs $1.54; FY2026 guidance $6.15-$6.45 per share reaffirmed; regulated earned ROE 9.3%

quarterly_data.signal: CONTRACTED LOAD RISES TO 63 GW through 2030, up from 56 GW last quarter, after AEP 'contracted an additional 7 GW of load coming mostly from AEP Texas and AEP Ohio.' CEO Bill Fehrman: 'Of the 63 GW, nearly 90% are data centers which include hyperscalers, while the rest are industrials.' 53 GW are in Texas and Ohio and need large-scale transmission; the remaining 10 GW requires new generation. By region: PJM contracted load increased by approximately 1 gigawatt (mainly Ohio, substantially all backed by take-or-pay ESAs); SPP increased by approximately 1 GW, driven primarily by an Amazon data center project in Northwest Louisiana (almost half of incremental SPP load now on take-or-pay ESAs); ERCOT accounted for the majority of growth, rising to 41 GW from 36 GW. Customers must meet investment-grade credit, parent guarantees or other credit support. Mihalik: last fall's $72 billion capital plan was set alongside a 28 GW contracted-load outlook, so the jump to 63 GW 'really implies a meaningful upside to our current capital plan.'
quarterly_data.figure: 63 GW contracted load through 2030 (vs 56 GW last quarter; +7 GW); nearly 90% data centers; 53 GW in Texas and Ohio; ERCOT 41 GW (from 36 GW); PJM and SPP each up approximately 1 GW

quarterly_data.signal: ERCOT DEMAND DETAIL AND INTERCONNECTION QUEUE: all 41 GW of ERCOT contracted load meets Senate Bill 6 standards and is secured through executed LOAs (customers must secure land, complete interconnection studies and fully fund related construction costs). In the April 1 RTP filing AEP Texas submitted 31 GW of incremental demand by end of decade and has since executed LOAs for another 10 GW; this is 'backed by roughly 60 GW of active load in the ERCOT interconnection queue.' Timing 'remains highly dependent on the supporting generation' — 'the question is not whether the demand exists, but when it comes online in ERCOT.' Across AEP, Fehrman: 'We now have 190 GW in our queue of people wanting to interconnect with us'. Beyond the forecast: a 10 GW data center campus with SB Energy in Piketon, Ohio (majority of its load not yet in the forecast) and a multi-billion dollar Google data center development in Putnam County, West Virginia that AEP is evaluating (early stage, not in the load forecast or financial outlook).
quarterly_data.figure: ERCOT: 31 GW submitted in RTP filing + another 10 GW of LOAs; roughly 60 GW ERCOT queue; 190 GW AEP interconnection queue; 10 GW Piketon campus with SB Energy (not in forecast)

quarterly_data.signal: FIVE-YEAR CAPITAL PLAN RAISED TO $78 BILLION from the prior $72 billion, driving an expected 11% five-year rate base CAGR and lifting the expected long-term operating earnings CAGR to greater than 9%. The $6 billion increase comprises $3.5 billion of recently approved PJM and SPP transmission investments (only ~$3.5 billion of roughly $5 billion of awards included; a conservative 50% assumption for the SPP line split with a regional peer) and two and a half billion dollars for I&M gas-fired generation (planned acquisition of the Sycamore and Big Sandy gas facilities); it is largely tied to projects entering service around 2029-2030. Transmission forecast now totals $33 billion (42% of the plan); generation capital outlook expanded by $3 billion to $24 billion through 2030. Line of sight to over $10 billion of projects outside the plan (Piketon Transmission Project, Wyoming Fuel Cell Initiative, additional generation) — Mihalik: Piketon and Wyoming alone 'could be around an $8 billion amount'. Capital plan has grown at roughly a 22% CAGR over the last four years; full update on the 3rd quarter call.
quarterly_data.figure: $78 billion 2026-2030 capital plan (up from $72 billion); $3.5 billion transmission + two and a half billion dollars I&M gas generation; transmission $33 billion (42%); generation $24 billion; over $10 billion upside projects (around an $8 billion from Piketon and Wyoming)

quarterly_data.signal: NEW 765 kV TRANSMISSION AWARDS: in SPP, AEP was directly assigned 315 miles of 765 kV lines from Seminole, Oklahoma, to Southwest Shreveport, Louisiana, plus projects from Potter, Texas, to Beckham County, Oklahoma — together $1.6 billion, in service by 2030. In PJM, AEP won the build-out of 330 miles of predominantly 765 kV lines in Ohio and Indiana ($1.9 billion, in service toward the end of the five-year plan). AEP was also selected for a nearly 200-mile 765 kV project in MISO (Wisconsin), in service 2034. AEP owns and operates more than 2,100 miles of 765 kV lines across six states; Fehrman credits the Quanta Services strategic partnership ('we know we have the labor to get it built') and new designs that reduce right of way and structure weight.
quarterly_data.figure: SPP 315 miles 765 kV + Potter–Beckham = $1.6 billion; PJM 330 miles = $1.9 billion; MISO nearly 200-mile project (2034); more than 2,100 miles of 765 kV owned

quarterly_data.signal: LONG-LEAD EQUIPMENT ALREADY SECURED: Fehrman says AEP is 'already securing extra high voltage, long lead time equipment like transformers, breakers, and lattice steel' and has 'secured more than 10 GW of gas-fired turbine capacity' from leading manufacturers; 'we are well ahead on our supply chain and the procurement for all of these projects that carry us out through this plan.' On turbines: 'we're most active with Mitsubishi and GE on the supply. We do have access to turbines going well out into the future'; pricing is under confidentiality agreements. AEP is building both simple cycle and combined cycle projects across its 11-state footprint, and is also evaluating nuclear sites (any investment conditional on loan guarantees and long-lead equipment support).
quarterly_data.figure: more than 10 GW of gas-fired turbine capacity secured; turbine pricing not disclosed (confidentiality agreements)

quarterly_data.signal: WYOMING FUEL-CELL PROJECT (with Bloom) AND BRIDGING POWER: Fehrman is 'confident that that project will continue forward' and says 'hopefully this will all get resolved by the end of the 2nd quarter' (work remains between other parties); AEP is 'doing a little bit of earthwork' and 'continuing to work with Bloom to ensure that we can meet the schedules that the customers want to have'. Mihalik on downside protection: if the project does not proceed AEP can put the fuel cells back to the hyperscaler at cost plus, 'roughly 10%'; the deadline is end of June, then a further six-month period for the hyperscaler to find another location anywhere in the U.S., after which AEP 'can put those fuel cells to the hyperscaler at 110%.' More broadly AEP offers bridging strategies to large loads — fuel cells, aeroderivatives and smaller interconnections.
quarterly_data.figure: fuel cells can be put back to the hyperscaler at 110% (cost plus roughly 10%); customer deadline end of June plus a six-month relocation period

quarterly_data.signal: RTO FRUSTRATION — PJM AND SPP MEMBERSHIP UNDER REVIEW: Fehrman says PJM's performance and stakeholder process give him little confidence interconnection delays will be fixed soon ('if something is not done now, I expect we could still be having these same conversations in 10 years') and AEP is 'assessing all of our options', with a similar review of SPP membership. In Q&A he clarified 'we're not saying we're exiting PJM' — the evaluation is at a very early stage and covers staying, shifting or alternative structures; SPP 'has been more aggressive in getting after these issues.' AEP may bid into the PJM reliability backstop through its unregulated business, and is studying a GenCo model for West Virginia (the governor's 50 GW by 2050 vision).

FINANCING AND REGULATORY BACKDROP: growth equity in the 2026-2030 plan raised by $1.1 billion to $7 billion — only 18% of the $6 billion incremental capital versus a typical 30%-40% industry equity content; $665 million of ATM equity already issued at an average price of over $131 per share, two-thirds of 2026 equity needs (plan: $1 billion ATM in 2026, none in 2027, $1 billion a year in 2028-2030). Operating cash flow forecast of over $47 billion over five years. S&P FFO to debt 14.7% and Moody's 13.9% versus a 14%-15% target. Federal support: $315 million in generation and distribution grants and a closed $1.6 billion DOE loan guarantee for transmission (over $275 million in projected customer savings). Large-load tariffs approved in Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky and West Virginia, with active filings in Michigan, Oklahoma, Texas and Virginia; Ohio ROE 9.84% (from 9.7%), Arkansas 9.65% (from 9.5%), West Virginia 9.75% (from 9.25%).
quarterly_data.figure: growth equity $7 billion (+$1.1 billion; 18% of incremental capex); $665 million ATM at over $131 per share; S&P FFO/debt 14.7%, Moody's 13.9%; $1.6 billion DOE loan guarantee; $315 million grants
